correctness.rationale: For n>=3, no-winner tournaments are the complement of n pairwise disjoint star faces, each fixing n-1 orientation bits. Exact character orthogonality proves all nonzero Walsh coefficients and all zero frequencies, with cancellation of singleton-edge coefficients. The inverse Fourier transform of the support indicator gives the exact graph kernel 2^(n-1) H(G)+4 e(G)-n^2+1. Translation averaging of arbitrary linear projections onto the translation-invariant convolution range proves the Fourier projection has global minimum l1 and l-infinity norm. Isolation inclusion-exclusion proves the finite sum. For G(n,1/2), the isolated-vertex correction differs from n by at most 2 n^3 2^(-(n-1)), and the binomial CLT with second-moment uniform integrability proves the displayed limiting coefficient. The standalone exact-integer checker verifies 33864 Fourier positions at n=3..6 and the exact graph sum through n=20; these finite checks are not used as an infinite proof.

originality.rationale: The specific all-frequency support and least endpoint projection norm for the natural no-Condorcet-winner orientation support are not implied by the inspected tournament-selection or score-geometry papers, by the known abstract translation-averaging mechanism, or by general full-Fourier-transform operator norms. The novelty assessment is qualified by bounded literature and indexed-record access, and cannot exclude an unindexed historical character-weighted formula.
residual_risks: Historical literature may have an unindexed or differently named full edge-star Fourier classification or the exact range-projection constant.
Two relevant general harmonic-analysis papers were compared on abstracts only; a stronger applicable specialized statement in their inaccessible full texts cannot be definitively excluded.
Results have undergone same-model review only and not independent mathematical validation.

value.rationale: The minimal real or complex l1/linfinity norm among all projections onto the winner-free tournament convolution range is a natural sharp Banach-space invariant, not a routine count. The Fourier range is extremely sparse but the endpoint projection constant grows linearly with an explicit, nonobvious coefficient. Its Gaussian contribution and isolated-vertex rare-event contribution remain of equal linear order, requiring both a CLT and delicate event conditioning. The exact graph-isolation formula is useful for finite benchmark calculations and may motivate analogous orientation constraints. The result is an all-n structural theorem rather than an arbitrary finite slice.
